description_full: CBL & Associates Properties, Inc. is headquartered in Chattanooga, TN, CBL Properties owns and manages a national portfolio of market-dominant properties located in dynamic and growing communities. CBL's owned and managed portfolio is comprised of 88 properties totaling 54.5 million square feet across 23 states, including 54 high-quality enclosed malls, outlet centers and lifestyle retail centers as well as more than 20 open-air centers and other assets. CBL seeks to continuously strengthen its company and portfolio through active management, aggressive leasing and profitable reinvestment in its properties. CBL & Associates Properties, Inc. was established in 1978n and was incorporated in Delaware.

financial_summary: CBL & Associates Properties, In is a small-cap real estate business with a $1.7B market cap on $578M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and -6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 12.9× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 1.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.6% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 12% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.5) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $122.5M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Carries more leverage than most Real Estate peers — a smaller cushion for the inevitable bad year
Interest-rate sensitivity and tenant-credit risk — cap rates and refinancing costs move faster than the 10-year leases can absorb.
Remote work structural vacancy — the post-pandemic shift to hybrid work has permanently impaired demand for urban office space across most markets.
Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

sector_tailwinds: Valued at a 33% discount to sector median EV/EBITDA
Returns on capital have been remarkably steady for 5 years — durability is the real test of a moat
Piotroski score 7/9 — financials improving across profitability, leverage and efficiency
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Financial quality scores above most Real Estate peers

sect: The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 57% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 30% and a beta of 0.85, it moves roughly with the market.
About $11.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 34% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades only 8% below its blended-model fair value of $59.42, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 17%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Real Estate peers: P/E 11.2 vs 23.9 and EV/EBITDA 10.8 vs 16.2 (sector median).
The Street target $66.00 on average, 21% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.02).
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.84x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 43%.
ROE of 36% is amplified by 7.3x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 2.9% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 12.9x net debt to EBITDA ($42.3M of cash against $2.2B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 1.8x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.48 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 0.9% over 3 years, 0.1% over 5 years and -5.8% over 10 years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.02, a backlog worth 20% of annual revenue and FFO growth of 13.4% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.2x depreciation (7.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own 12.0%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 78%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (15 sales, net $122.5M sold).
It returns 5.6% a year to shareholders (1.1% in buybacks and 4.6% in dividends).
The share count has grown 8.3% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 408 employees, each generates about $1.4M of revenue, 0.6x the Real Estate median, and revenue has fallen 4.3% a year across its filed history.
CEO pay is $2.9M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
